suggestions.issue: <section> #1 has no <title> — recommended for DITA compliance
context_lines: Abstract: This section covers the Table style in HTML — the primary structure for presenting information with inherent row-and-column relationships — and ten scenarios: a standard multi-column table, a table with a caption, a table with no header row, merged cells, nested tables, lists and images inside table cells, tables spanning multiple pages, consecutive tables, and a two-column parameter table in a reference topic. The converter reads each table's structure, cell complexity, and topic context to determine whether to map it to <simpletable>, a CALS <table>, or <properties>.

ATable is the primary structure for reference and lookup content. It is a structural mechanism to present information that has inherent row-and-column relationships — parameter names and their values, feature names and their states, error codes and their meanings, API fields and their data types.

A table reduces a lookup task from reading a paragraph to scanning a row and column. In DITA-XML, a table is structured data — each cell is a discrete, addressable unit that a transform can reformat for PDF, or online help output, filter by column for conditional publishing, and extract independently for reuse in other deliverables.

A table is an HTML structure used to organize related information into rows and columns. Represented by the native <table> element together with <tr>, <th>, and <td>, it presents information that is easier to compare, scan, or reference than the same information written as continuous text. Tables commonly represent configuration parameters, feature comparisons, error codes, API fields, and other structured lookup information.

suggestions.issue: <section> #1 has no <title> — recommended for DITA compliance
context_lines: Abstract: This section covers the Table of Contents and Root Index — the navigation structure that maps the publication hierarchy and serves as the converter's primary entry point for building the root DITA map — and two scenarios: a root index file present in the package, and a missing root index file. The converter reads the root index to construct the DITA map hierarchy and topic references; when no root index is present, it falls back to the package folder name or filename as the root map title.

A table of contents or root index is the navigation structure of a publication. It declares the document's complete hierarchy in one place — the titles, sequence, and parent-child relationships of all sections, chapters, and topics — and provides the entry point from which readers and systems navigate the entire deliverable.

For the publishing system, the table of contents or root index is the structural anchor of the entire output — every generated navigation artifact, including the PDF bookmark panel, the HTML5 navigation tree, the WebHelp TOC panel, and the DITA map hierarchy, derives from this structure.

NOTE: The converter reads it to build the DITA map hierarchy and then discards it — the publishing transform regenerates the navigation structure at build time from the assembled DITA map, ensuring it always reflects the actual content rather than a manually maintained list that can fall out of sync.

suggestions.issue: <section> #1 has no <title> — recommended for DITA compliance
context_lines: A reference section is recognized by a noun-phrase heading containing a lookup keyword such as "Supported File Formats," "Error Codes," or "API Parameters," paired with a table or parameter list as the dominant body structure. The heading keyword is the primary classification signal. A section containing only a table but no lookup keyword in the heading may be classified as Concept or Generic depending on the surrounding context.

When these signals align, the converter generates a <reference> element with <refbody>. The opening paragraph maps to <shortdesc>. Any introductory prose appearing before the first table is wrapped in a <section> element inside <refbody> rather than placed directly in <refbody>. A 2-column table in a section whose heading contains an API keyword such as "API," "parameters," "fields," or "attributes" maps to <properties>. The same 2-column table in a reference section without an API keyword maps to <simpletable>.
The following scenarios demonstrate how different HTML reference patterns are interpreted during HTML-to-DITA conversion:
suggestions.suggestion:
#1 has no — recommended for DITA compliance. Add a `<title>` element as the first child of the `<section>` element. Example: `<section><title>Section Title

...

`
